title: System Design & WebRTC Under the Hood Explained ⚡
ig_caption:
System Design & Software Architecture Explained ⚡ How WebRTC connects peers through NAT!
Your friend sits behind TWO locked routers—and the call still finds them.

• WebRTC = real-time media over the internet (low-latency)
• Web RTC handshake: find an addressable path to the peer
• STUN server: discovers your public-facing network info (NAT mapping)
• Matchmaker: coordinates who talks to whom (signaling)
• TURN relay: fallback when direct paths fail (media relayed via server)
• Router · NAT: blocks inbound connections → WebRTC adapts
• Typical target latency budget: ~80 ms for responsive voice/video

Practical takeaway: In interviews, describe the pipeline as “signaling → ICE candidate gathering → connectivity checks → P2P if possible, TURN otherwise.”

Question: If you had to pick one in production—STUN-only vs TURN fallback—what would you optimize for: cost, latency, or reliability?

fb_caption:
WebRTC is the system-design interview favorite because it’s a full end-to-end story: addressing, discovery, NAT traversal, and media transport—under real latency constraints.

Under the hood, a typical WebRTC call looks like this:

1) Signaling / Matchmaking (out-of-band)
- Participants must learn “who is who” and exchange session metadata (SDP, ICE parameters).
- In practice, this is handled by a matchmaker + signaling channel (often WebSocket-based).
- Trade-off: signaling servers scale differently than media forwarding. Keep them lightweight and stateless where possible.

2) ICE Candidate Gathering
- Each client enumerates possible network paths.
- STUN helps discover the public address/port mapping created by NAT.
- Trade-off: STUN improves success rates for direct connectivity, but does not guarantee it.

3) Connectivity Checks (ICE)
- Peers test which candidate pairs work.
- If a direct path exists, WebRTC establishes a P2P connection.
- If traversal fails due to restrictive NAT/firewalls, the system must fall back.

4) TURN Relay (the “just connect” fallback)
- TURN relays media through a server when P2P is impossible.
- Trade-off: TURN increases cost and adds relay latency, but maximizes reliability.
- Production lesson: design policies—e.g., attempt P2P first, escalate to TURN only when needed.

Architecture patterns & system lessons:
- Separate control plane (signaling/matchmaking) from data plane (media path).
- Embrace multi-path negotiation (ICE) rather than assuming one network topology.
- Budget latency carefully; real-time voice/video often targets ~80ms responsiveness in the user’s perception.
